title: I've worked at PC Gamer for 18 years. These are the 13 games on my Steam Wishlist
summary: If Steam is an ocean rising at a rate of 110 new games per day, this article is a snorkel.
body: I usually use Steam's wishlisting feature to make sure I don't forget about interesting projects that have open-ended development times, games like Anvil Empires that have been in development for years but still don't have a confirmed date. I'm looking forward to stuff like Dawn of War 4 and Divinity, but I don't tend to wishlist big, obvious games like this. My genres are first-person shooter, deckbuilders, and tactics, which you'll see favored here more than a little. Kriegsfront Tactics A spiritual successor to one of my favorite PlayStation series, Front Mission. I will forever believe that mechs make the best enemies, and the '70s Southeast Asia setting is fresh. Space Station 14 Endearingly old-school multiplayer story generator astro-sandbox. SS13 is one of DayZ creator Dean Hall's favorites, if that tells you something. Hull Rupture Spaceship tower defense with wonderfully intricate, cross-section pixel art. The third game in the quietly-growing Despot's game cinematic universe. Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Tactics Hot out of Gamescom. This will be the second Siege spinoff, if you remember Extraction. title: My first MMO character #7: Andrea Shearon
summary: My first MMO character #7: Andrea Shearon
body: My first MMO character was... Rennyfuu, Archer Born: ~2002-2006 Game: Priston Tale I spent time poking around in RuneScape and Graal Online as a kid, but they didn't stick. It wasn't until my failed campaign to persuade my mom into giving me her credit card for Final Fantasy 11 that I found my true MMO gateway: Priston Tale. The western release was in beta for years, and I spent most of that time lagging to death on a 4MB integrated GPU as the game's worst archer. I have fond memories of arguing with grown adults twice my age about winning strategies in Survive or Die—the game's big arena brawl against waves of monsters—and distinctly remember a thread on an old fan forum dedicated to complaining about me. I was a menace. I made multiple characters before Priston Tale eventually died out and was sold to Suba Games, where I'm fairly certain it remains active. I'm sure Rennyfuu is long gone by now, but sometimes I toy with the idea of going back for a visit. (Read the full article here)

title: Speaking to pro Counter-Strike players convinced me to finally increase my mouse's polling rate, but not all the way to 8K
summary: Maybe *this* will be what keeps me at FaceIt level 8...
body: Azuwu - CS2 player for Luminosity "I'd say there's a difference from 1 to 2K and then, after that, 8K you don't even reach anyway. So it's only 2K or 4K, but they're both fine. I play at 4K." yxngstxr - CS2 player for Luminosity "1K is the minimum. If you play 4K, it's going to be way smoother—not 'way' [smoother], but you will notice it. It's a smoother motion than if you put it at 1K... I'm on 800 [DPI], 1 kHz... because usually I like to flick." A couple of days ago I got the chance to speak with two pro Counter-Strike 2 players, Azuwu and yxngstxr , both from team Luminosity Gaming . Amongst other things, I asked them about polling rates. As a long-time (and recently-returned) Counter-Strike player, I've stuck to 1 kHz despite all the hype over 4K and 8K. I've tried 8K for comparison before and couldn't make out much of a difference. I've always stuck to 800 DPI and 1 kHz, just like yxngstxr, in my case mainly because it saves battery life and doesn't risk any lower performance or stuttering which is a risk with 8K on some systems. Our James recently tried out different polling rates and didn't find a consistent benefit, either. Here I am, talking to yxngstxr. (Image credit: F…

title: I made two $50 gaming keyboards fight for my average-gamer affections, and for me there's one clear winner

body: Welcome to my own personal battle of the budget gaming keyboards, where I make two reasonably-priced input devices fight to the bitter end for my affections. Okay, so it's more about working out which one I'd actually spend my money on, but that hasn't got the same ring to it. Onwards! In the left corner sits the Gamakay x NaughShark NS68 , a keeb with the silliest name I've ever heard. Still, it's got a surprisingly good specs sheet for its $40 MSRP, although it's gone up since our review and is now often found for $50-$60 instead. It's been our best budget gaming keyboard pick for a while now, mostly because its value proposition is damn hard to beat for the cash—even with the price increase. However, warming up in the right corner is the new kid on the block; the Razer Reclusa X Mini 65% is so fresh to the market, it hasn't even started shaving yet. But, being a proper mechanical mini keeb with a $50 price tag , it's sure swinging for the fences straight out of the gate. Something like that, anyway. title: My first MMO character #6: Jacob Ridley
summary: My first MMO character #6: Jacob Ridley
body: My first MMO character was... Don L Legs Born: [I was a small child] Game: RuneScape My memories from this time are hazy at best. If this is all bollocks to a seasoned RuneScape player, this is at least what I thought was happening at the time. I was very young, but I think I remember a few things. I got really good at fishing. Like, really good. I was top level or something like that. Fishing and cooking. I used my skills to trade cooked fish with higher level players, and they'd give me good armour. I always wanted the black armour with golden highlights, whatever that was, and I got it by becoming a virtual fishmonger. I also got a red face mask and a black halberd. It was wicked. One day, I just stopped playing. You don't realise it's the last time you'll play, but it was—at least for a very long time. I always kept my account details, though. Not too long ago, in 2025, I decided to log back in after God knows how many years. I'm 34 now, but I was 33 then. I must've been 10 or under when I was playing RuneScape. I was banned. My account had been banned for years. Some clown had stolen it and used it to do nefarious things in my name. I don't know why, but I felt a real sadness…

body: Day 1: Anybody home? (Image credit: Wild Forest Studio) I arrive at my grandpa's overgrown old cottage alone. Where's he run off to? Apparently I don't know. There's only enough time on day one to read several tutorial popups telling me what to do next (oh dear, that ta-dah noise is going to get on my nerves fast), cut a few trees with my axe so I can use wood to fix my bed, and go to sleep. Day 2: There's always free seeds Today I get to walk into town and oh, jeez, everyone here is Eeyore-level sad, heads facing navels and all. Even the music is depressing. The mayor tells me the town's in shambles and everyone's gone away and maybe I could help the couple folks who are left. Well then, it's time to roll up my farm simming sleeves. The merchant wants berries which I can pick a ton of growing wild on my farm. The carpenter wants me to fix a cart by chopping wood. The gardener wants me to try growing wheat on my farm. Done, done, and done! In the midst of doing all that though, I'm surprised by which things Dragon Shelter considers worthy of popup explainers versus what goes completely unexplained without even an indicator in the interface. title: Experimental RPG developer Summer Eternal: 'We're giving away 5% of our studio to you, the Players' in order to 'mend the trust broken in this industry a thousand times over'
summary: Maybe it's time for something new.
body: Summer Eternal is an RPG studio co-founded by ex-ZA/UM designers Argo Tuulik and Dora Klindžić, as well as developer/organizer Aleksandar Gavrilović (quoted above). Given the former two developers' experience working on a canceled Disco Elysium expansion , it makes sense they'd want to try something radically different for their new studio's financing and governance. Worker-owned cooperatives are rare but not unheard-of in games, but Summer Eternal is also looking to offer ownership stakes (and profit sharing) to its freelancers and customers. Crucially, it's not in the form of "walkin' around money" for the latter group. Instead, Summer Eternal wants to offer players a democratic say in the studio's direction, backed up by control of 5% of the profits. It reminds me of the EVE Online Council of Stellar Management or Old School RuneScape's player voting on new features, but with this added element of the studio literally putting its money where its mouth is. At a time when traditionally governed, publicly-traded games companies are cannibalizing themselves before our eyes to fulfil a fiduciary duty to their shareholders, such an economically and politically radical proposition mig…

I do remember a wee bit about what I was doing at university, though, and that was mostly playing World of Warcraft, Star Wars Galaxies and Guild Wars. My buddy Zarwulf had a big sword, an impressive grimace, and probably a pet wolf. And he still exists, frozen in time—a situation I'm not going to remedy by playing him again. title: PC Gamer's Hyperfeed beta is live
summary: We're testing a beta version of our homepage. Let us know what you think!
body: Mind our dust! And don't let any of it get into your PC's fans. We're temporarily testing a new version of the PC Gamer homepage called the Hyperfeed that you'll see getting lots of updates over at pcgamer.com/hyperfeed . This is a very early, pre-pre-proto-alpha test, a minimum-viable version for early data gathering and experimentation. You'll notice a bug or three as we continue to iterate. Why are we trying something new? The impact of Google's coercive integration of AI has affected the online publishing ecosystem a lot, and we're trying to make our homepage (already the most-visited page on PC Gamer) a much richer experience. We're excited to modernize pcgamer.com in a way that better reflects how you and we play. Apart from a different look, the main thing you'll notice are short, ephemeral posts currently only found on the Hyperfeed. Gaming in 2026 is so often about the microscopic stuff: character abilities, individual voice lines, a fun character you cooked up in an RPG, two minutes of one session you had in ARC Raiders, a weird ice-poison wand you looted in Diablo 4. We want to talk about our observations and feelings on these small-but-significant things by giving ours…

title: I cannot believe this obscure MMO from my childhood is still going 23 years later
summary: Was I always this bad at it, though?
body: I grew up in the 2000s with a PC but not a whole lot of money. That's the kind of combination that gets you bargain-bin Sold Out Software games from Poundland or, more so in my case, an absurd number of free-to-play online and browser-based games that were utterly pervasive across the internet. My childhood was a never-ending revolving door of these mid-tier Flash and Java games. Some have long left my memory, a fleeting experience. But some continue to rattle around in my brain, reminding me of simpler times where I didn't have to pay taxes or subject myself to at least one hour of screen-free time before bed lest I wake up with a headache the next morning. But where are these weird and wonderful games now? Are they still scattered across the internet? Are they in their original forms, practically untouched, or have they evolved into far deeper and darker games than they once were? Well, as I continue to march into my 30s against my will, I've been thinking back to the games I would play as a child and asking myself just that question. title: Where to find the Shimanoyama region Treasure Hunt in Forza Horizon 6
summary: Smash this chest beside a snowy road.
body: This week there's another challenge to complete in Forza Horizon 6 . This time we've got the Shimanoyama Treasure Hunt to track down, and doing it will grant you some season progress. The British Automotive Festival Series is currently underway and there are a couple of season reward cars to grab, namely the Vauxhall Astra VXR and Bentley Bentayga. Finding and smashing this chest will get you a little closer to earning them. title: My first MMO character #4: Lincoln Carpenter
summary: My first MMO character #4: Lincoln Carpenter
body: My first MMO character was... Maldirr, Orc Warrior Born: ~2005 Game: World of Warcraft Technically, my very first MMO characters were in a RuneScape account (that was later hacked during years of inactivity) and a Trandoshan force-sensitive in Star Wars Galaxies, that I only played long enough to realize the New Game Enhancements were bad. After enough hours of watching cinematic raid clear videos on WarcraftMovies.com and daydreaming about the legendary weapon names I saw after Googling my way to Thottbot, I convinced my parents to foot the bill for a WoW subscription. My intention was to make an Orc hunter. I misclicked. I only realized I was playing a warrior after noticing my new character didn't have a bow. But I rolled with it, and Maldirr remained my WoW main for years, Mortal Striking his way through casual Arms DPS rotations across somewhere in the neighborhood of four expansions. Eventually, however, the thrill of big Execute numbers gave way to other curiosities, and I started putting more time into my Worgen rogue. Then my undead mage.
